cloze.text: Pericoronitis is inflammation of the soft-tissue flap ({{c1::operculum}}) overlying a {{c2::partially erupted}} tooth.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: think of "peri" as "peeking out" — a tooth that is peeking out (erupting).

cloze.text: Pericoronitis is caused by {{c1::bacteria, food debris, and trauma}} in the flap of tissue over a partially erupted tooth.
Pericoronitis most commonly affects the {{c1::mandibular third molars}} (hard to clean).
Pericoronitis appears as {{c1::swollen, red}} tissue covering a partially erupted tooth and can have {{c2::pus}}.
Symptoms of pericoronitis: pain, foul taste, bad breath, and limited jaw opening ({{c1::trismus}}).
cloze.extra: The book's treatment sentence for pericoronitis is cut off ("Treated with…").

cloze.text: Impetigo is a highly contagious bacterial skin infection caused by {{c1::Staphylococcus aureus}} or {{c2::Streptococcus pyogenes}}.
Impetigo most commonly affects {{c1::young children}} in close-contact settings like schools or daycares.
Impetigo is typically located around the {{c1::nose and mouth}}.
In impetigo, vesicles or bullae rupture and form {{c1::golden-yellow (honey-colored)}} crusts.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: "impetigo" = "I'm pretty gold" — golden crusts that look like gold flakes, but infected.

cloze.text: Impetigo is {{c1::not painful}} (may be itchy or tender) and is treated with {{c2::antibiotics}}.
Strep throat is a bacterial infection caused by Streptococcus pyogenes ({{c1::Group A}} Streptococcus).
Strep throat is most often seen in children {{c1::5–15}} years old, but can occur at any age.
Strep throat is highly contagious; it spreads through {{c1::respiratory droplets}} or contaminated surfaces.
Oral signs of strep throat: {{c1::petechiae}} (tiny red dots) on the soft palate and a {{c2::strawberry tongue}} (red and bumpy).
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: strep sounds like straw — strawberry: bright red, bumpy tongue.

cloze.text: Strep throat can progress to {{c1::scarlet fever}} (bright red, sandpaper-like rash) or {{c2::rheumatic fever}}.
Strep throat symptoms: sore throat, fever, swollen tonsils with {{c1::white patches}}, and tender neck lymph nodes; treated with {{c2::antibiotics}}.
Actinomycosis is a chronic bacterial infection caused by {{c1::Actinomyces}}, filamentous {{c2::gram-positive}} bacteria.
Actinomyces are generally harmless in the mouth; they cause actinomycosis when they reach deeper tissues through {{c1::trauma, surgery, or dental procedures}}.
Actinomycosis is most common in the {{c1::cervicofacial}} region (jaw, face, neck), especially after dental infections or extractions.
Actinomycosis appears as firm abscesses that drain through {{c1::sinus tracts}}, releasing thick {{c2::yellow}} pus.
Actinomycosis is treated with long-term antibiotics (usually {{c1::penicillin}}) and surgical drainage.
Verruca vulgaris spreads by direct contact, often from skin to mouth through habits like {{c1::finger-sucking or nail-biting}}.
cloze.extra: Lesson: wash your hands!

cloze.text: Verruca vulgaris is most common on the {{c1::lips}}, but may also be on the labial mucosa or tongue.
Verruca vulgaris is a {{c1::white}}, painless, exophytic lesion with a {{c2::papillary or cauliflower-like}} surface.
Verruca vulgaris is treated by {{c1::surgical excision}}.
Condyloma acuminatum is a benign papillary lesion caused by HPV, most commonly types {{c1::6 and 11}}.
Condyloma acuminatum is transmitted primarily through {{c1::sexual contact}}.
Oral condyloma acuminatum occurs on the {{c1::tongue, buccal mucosa, gingiva, palate, or alveolar ridge}}.
Condyloma acuminatum: soft, {{c1::pink}}, finger-like or cauliflower-like projections — usually larger, more diffuse and {{c2::multiple}}.
cloze.extra: Contrast: verruca vulgaris is solitary and white. WakeUpMemory: Condylo sounds like "cauliflower" — big, bumpy, soft-pink growths.

cloze.text: Condyloma acuminatum is treated by surgical excision; {{c1::recurrence}} can occur.
Candidiasis (oral thrush) is caused by overgrowth of the fungus {{c1::Candida albicans}}.

Candidiasis develops especially when the {{c1::immune system is weakened}} (infants, elderly, HIV, cancer, diabetes) or the {{c2::oral flora is disrupted}} (antibiotics, corticosteroids, dry mouth, poor denture hygiene).
Candidiasis can occur in both {{c1::dry and moist}} environments.
Classic candidiasis: {{c1::white, creamy plaques that wipe off}}, leaving a {{c2::red, raw base}}.
{{c1::Erythematous}} candidiasis shows red, burning areas with no white plaque, often under dentures.
cloze.extra: Don't be confused: candidiasis is not always white — don't rule out Candida just because there's no white stuff!

cloze.text: {{c1::Angular cheilitis}} (cracked corners of the mouth) is often associated with Candida, especially in denture wearers or nutritional deficiencies.
Symptoms of candidiasis: burning, soreness, {{c1::altered taste}}, and sensitivity to spicy or acidic foods.
Candidiasis is treated with topical antifungals ({{c1::nystatin, clotrimazole}}) or, in severe cases, systemic {{c2::fluconazole}}.
HSV-1 causes {{c1::oral}} infections; HSV-2 causes {{c2::oral and genital}} infections.
Primary herpetic gingivostomatitis is caused by {{c1::initial exposure}} to HSV-1, usually in children under {{c2::6}}.
Primary herpetic gingivostomatitis: painful, red, swollen gingiva and vesicles with {{c1::fever, malaise, and cervical lymphadenopathy}}; severity varies.
Primary herpetic gingivostomatitis spreads through {{c1::saliva or contact with infected lesions}} (e.g., toys, sharing a spoon with the caregiver).
Primary herpetic gingivostomatitis and recurrent herpes both heal on their own in {{c1::1–2 weeks}}; recurrent lesions heal {{c2::without scarring}}.
Recurrent herpes simplex is reactivation of latent HSV in the {{c1::trigeminal ganglion (CN V)}}.
Recurrent herpes is often triggered by {{c1::stress, sun exposure, menstruation, fatigue, or illness}}.
Recurrent herpes: clusters of tiny painful vesicles that rupture, often after {{c1::prodromal}} tingling, pain or burning {{c2::1–2 days}} before the vesicles appear.
Recurrent herpes lesions on the lip border are called {{c1::herpes labialis}} (cold sores).
Recurrent herpes is most contagious during the {{c1::vesicle}} stage, but virus can be shed even {{c2::without visible lesions}}.
Antiviral medications such as {{c1::acyclovir or valacyclovir}} treat herpes and may reduce severity.
Herpes on the finger is called {{c1::herpetic whitlow}}; herpes on the eyes is {{c2::ocular (ophthalmic)}} herpes.
Aphthous ulcers are caused by {{c1::immune-related factors, stress, trauma, or an unknown trigger}} (not a virus).

Aphthous ulcers occur on {{c1::movable, non-keratinized}} mucosa (labial and buccal mucosa, soft palate, ventral tongue); recurrent herpetic ulcers occur on {{c2::keratinized, attached}} mucosa (hard palate, attached gingiva).
An aphthous ulcer looks like a {{c1::yellowish-white ulcer with a red halo}}; herpetic ulcers are a {{c2::cluster of small ulcers following vesicle rupture}}.
Aphthous ulcer sizes: minor {{c1::less than 1 cm}}; major {{c2::more than 1 cm}}; herpetiform {{c3::1–2 mm clusters}}.
Minor aphthous ulcers heal in {{c1::7–10 days}}; major aphthous ulcers take {{c2::weeks (may scar)}}; herpetic ulcers usually heal in 7–14 days.
Aphthous ulcers respond to {{c1::topical steroids}}; herpetiform aphthous ulcers to {{c2::tetracycline}}.
{{c1::Varicella-zoster virus (VZV)}} causes both chickenpox (varicella) and shingles (herpes zoster); a {{c2::vaccine}} is available for prevention.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: "virus" is Latin for poison — tiny invaders that hijack your cells to multiply.

cloze.text: Chickenpox is most common in {{c1::children}} and spreads by respiratory droplets or direct contact with lesions.
Chickenpox appears as {{c1::itchy, fluid-filled vesicles}} on the skin, often with fever, malaise and fatigue.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: "varicella" comes from Latin "varius" = speckled — like the itchy blisters of chickenpox.

cloze.text: Chickenpox resolves in {{c1::7–10 days}} and does not necessarily need treatment unless the patient is {{c2::immunocompromised}}.
Shingles is caused by {{c1::reactivation}} of dormant varicella-zoster virus.
Shingles is seen in {{c1::older adults}} or those with weakened immune systems.
Shingles: {{c1::unilateral}}, painful vesicles that follow a {{c2::dermatome}} (nerve path).
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: "zoster" comes from Greek for belt — shingles wraps around the body like a belt.

cloze.text: Shingles is painful and can take {{c1::weeks to months}} to heal; it is treated with antiviral medication, pain medicine, and {{c2::steroids}}.
The {{c1::Coxsackie}} virus, a member of the {{c2::enterovirus}} family, causes both herpangina and hand-foot-mouth disease.
There is {{c1::no specific antiviral}} treatment for Coxsackie virus infections.
Herpangina affects the {{c1::posterior}} oral cavity: soft palate, tonsillar pillars, uvula, and throat.
Herpangina appears as {{c1::small red spots or ulcers}}.
Herpangina spreads through saliva, respiratory droplets, or the {{c1::fecal-oral}} route.
Herpangina causes fever, sore throat, headache, and {{c1::loss of appetite}}; it resolves in 7–10 days.
Hand-foot-mouth disease affects the tongue and buccal mucosa and the skin of the {{c1::palms and soles}} (sometimes buttocks); it is most common in children under {{c2::5}}.
Hand-foot-mouth disease: {{c1::painful oral ulcers}} and red spots or blisters on the skin, with oral pain, mild fever, fatigue and rash.
Hand-foot-mouth disease is managed with {{c1::supportive care}} (hydration, rest, fever control) and resolves in 7–10 days.

Erythema multiforme is an acute {{c1::immune-mediated hypersensitivity}} reaction, commonly triggered by {{c2::herpes simplex infection}} or medications such as antibiotics, anticonvulsants, and NSAIDs.
Erythema multiforme affects the skin and the oral mucosa, especially the {{c1::lateral tongue and lips}}.
Erythema multiforme: {{c1::target (bull's-eye)}} skin lesions with concentric rings, oral ulcers, and {{c2::crusted, bleeding lips}}.
Erythema multiforme has a {{c1::sudden and explosive}} onset; if severe, it requires medical intervention.

{{c1::Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS)}} is a life-threatening, severe form of erythema multiforme (some consider it a distinct disorder) with extensive blistering, necrosis and sloughing of skin and mucosa; it requires {{c2::hospitalization}}.
Lichen planus is a {{c1::benign}}, chronic inflammatory condition affecting the skin and oral mucosa.
cloze.extra: Fun fact: Latin/Greek lichen = "moss" + planus = "flat" — a flat, moss-like appearance.

cloze.text: Lichen planus is most common on the {{c1::buccal mucosa}}.
In severe cases lichen planus may present as {{c1::erosive or ulcerative}} lesions.
Oral lichen planus is {{c1::bilateral and symmetrical}}.
Lichen planus is often asymptomatic but can be painful; it may require {{c1::corticosteroids}}.
cloze.extra: The book prints "Often symptomatic, but it can be painful" — almost certainly a typo for "asymptomatic".

cloze.text: Pemphigus vulgaris is a chronic {{c1::autoimmune}} disease that causes fragile, painful blisters on the skin and oral mucosa.
Pemphigus vulgaris forms {{c1::intraepithelial}} blisters due to {{c2::acantholysis}} (loss of adhesion between epithelial cells).
Conditions with a positive Nikolsky sign: {{c1::pemphigus vulgaris}} (classic and most important), {{c2::Stevens-Johnson syndrome}}, and sometimes {{c3::mucous membrane pemphigoid}}.
In pemphigus vulgaris, oral lesions often appear {{c1::before}} skin involvement.
Pemphigus vulgaris is painful and requires {{c1::biopsy}} and {{c2::immunosuppressive therapy}} (e.g., corticosteroids or biologics).
Mucous membrane pemphigoid is a chronic autoimmune disease causing {{c1::erosive lesions}} on mucous membranes (oral, ocular, genital); it is generally {{c2::less severe}} than pemphigus vulgaris.
cloze.extra: Fun fact: "pemphigoid" = Greek pemphix (blister/bubble) + -oid (resembling) = "blister-like".

cloze.text: Mucous membrane pemphigoid lesions often heal with {{c1::scarring}}.
Mucous membrane pemphigoid is most common on the gingiva, presenting as {{c1::desquamative gingivitis}} (peeling, inflamed gums).
Mucous membrane pemphigoid is painful; it requires {{c1::biopsy}} for diagnosis and is managed with {{c2::corticosteroids}}.
Cyclic neutropenia is a rare {{c1::inherited}} disorder with periodic decreases in neutrophil count every {{c2::21–27 days}}, lasting {{c3::2–3 days}}.
Cyclic neutropenia mostly affects the {{c1::gingiva}}; ulcers may also occur on the tongue, buccal mucosa, or palate.
Cyclic neutropenia causes painful ulcers and gingival inflammation during neutropenic episodes; tissue {{c1::heals between episodes}}.
Recurring cyclic neutropenia causes rapid {{c1::periodontal destruction}} and potential tooth loss.
Ellis-van Creveld syndrome is a rare genetic disorder inherited in an {{c1::autosomal recessive}} pattern.
In Ellis-van Creveld syndrome, tissue is fused to the upper lip from canine to canine, eliminating the {{c1::labial vestibule}}.
Ellis-van Creveld dental findings: missing {{c1::central incisors}}, a single {{c2::peg-shaped}} tooth in the center, and {{c3::natal teeth}} (teeth present at birth).
Ellis-van Creveld syndrome is linked to dwarfism, {{c1::polydactyly}} (extra fingers), and hypoplastic nails.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: EVC = Extra fingers, Vanishing vestibule, and a Central incisor that's gone.

cloze.text: Cleidocranial dysplasia is a genetic skeletal disorder affecting bone and tooth development, inherited {{c1::autosomal dominant}} (but can arise spontaneously).
cloze.extra: Fun fact: actor Gaten Matarazzo (Dustin in Stranger Things) has cleidocranial dysplasia and has spoken openly about his surgeries and dental challenges.

cloze.text: In cleidocranial dysplasia, absent or underdeveloped {{c1::clavicles}} let patients bring their shoulders together at the midline.
Cleidocranial dysplasia dental findings: multiple {{c1::supernumerary teeth}}, {{c2::delayed eruption}}, and pseudoanodontia.
Cleidocranial dysplasia is treated with {{c1::extractions and orthodontic intervention}}.
Treacher Collins syndrome (mandibulofacial dysostosis) is caused by abnormal development of the {{c1::first and second pharyngeal (branchial) arches}}.
Treacher Collins syndrome especially affects the {{c1::zygomatic bones}} and {{c2::mandible}}, giving a sunken midface, high palate and downward-slanting mouth corners (fish-like appearance).
Treacher Collins syndrome: underdeveloped cheekbones and {{c1::micrognathia}} (small jaw), with malocclusion, open bite, cleft palate, and mouth breathing.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: TCS = Tiny Cheeks + Sunken Chin.

cloze.text: Treacher Collins syndrome causes {{c1::hearing loss}} due to malformed middle ear ossicles.
The {{c1::oral cavity}} is often one of the first places signs of HIV appear, so oral lesions help with early detection, disease monitoring, and timely referral.
{{c1::Candidiasis}} is a common opportunistic infection in HIV/AIDS, appearing as white plaques that wipe off, red patches, or angular cheilitis.
Hairy leukoplakia appears as white, corrugated plaques on the {{c1::lateral tongue}} that {{c2::do not wipe off}}; it may be the first visible sign of HIV.
Kaposi sarcoma is a {{c1::purple}} vascular tumor, often on the palate or gingiva, almost exclusive to {{c2::late-stage}} HIV.
Linear gingival erythema is a red band along the gingival margin that is {{c1::not associated with plaque}}; it relates more to immune dysregulation than bacterial irritation.
In HIV, {{c1::major aphthous ulcers}} are larger and more painful than typical canker sores and take weeks to heal, often with scarring.
In HIV, herpes simplex lesions may persist for more than {{c1::14}} days and appear more severe.
Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a chronic autoimmune disease affecting the skin, joints, kidneys and other organs that worsens with {{c1::sun exposure}} (photosensitivity).
SLE oral lesions most often affect the {{c1::buccal mucosa, palate, and lips}}.
Oral SLE: red, ulcerated areas or white, lacy striations that may resemble {{c1::lichen planus}}.
SLE symptoms: fatigue, {{c1::joint pain}}, and immune suppression.
Behçet syndrome is a rare autoimmune {{c1::vasculitis}} that causes inflammation in blood vessels.
Behçet syndrome causes {{c1::recurrent large, deeper, painful}} ulcers on the oral mucosa, often the soft palate, lips, tongue, or buccal mucosa.
Behçet syndrome classic triad: {{c1::oral ulcers}}, {{c2::genital ulcers}}, and {{c3::ocular inflammation}}.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: Behçet sounds like "bite set" — a set of 3 painful spots: mouth (where you bite), genitals, and eyes.

cloze.text: Papillon-Lefèvre syndrome is a rare {{c1::genetic}} disorder that begins in early childhood, with both oral and skin manifestations.
cloze.extra: Named after two French physicians, Dr. Papillon and Dr. Paul Lefèvre, who described it in 1924 — not after the butterfly (French "papillon").

cloze.text: Papillon-Lefèvre syndrome causes severe {{c1::periodontitis}} with early loss of teeth, often by age {{c2::14}}.
Papillon-Lefèvre syndrome's key skin feature is {{c1::palmar and plantar hyperkeratosis}} (thickened skin on hands and feet).
Gardner syndrome is a genetic disorder that causes multiple {{c1::osteomas}} (benign bone growths), particularly in the jaw and skull.
Gardner syndrome: multiple {{c1::radiopaque}} osteomas, impacted or unerupted teeth, {{c2::hypercementosis}}, and crowding.
Gardner syndrome's systemic feature is intestinal {{c1::polyps}} with a high risk of malignancy.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: in Gardner syndrome the garden grows rocks (osteomas) and too much cement (hypercementosis) — but beware, some weeds (colon polyps) can turn deadly.

cloze.text: Syphilis is a sexually transmitted infection caused by the spirochete {{c1::Treponema pallidum}}; oral findings vary by stage.
Primary syphilis occurs about {{c1::3 weeks}} after exposure, at the site of infection.
The oral lesion of primary syphilis is the {{c1::chancre}} — a single, firm, round, {{c2::painless}} ulcer.
Primary syphilis is highly infectious; the chancre heals spontaneously in {{c1::2–4 weeks}} but still needs antibiotic treatment ({{c2::penicillin}}).
Secondary syphilis occurs about {{c1::6 weeks}} after the primary lesion heals.
The oral lesion of secondary syphilis is {{c1::mucous patches}} — multiple, painless, grayish-white plaques on ulcerated mucosa.
Tertiary syphilis is the late stage of untreated syphilis, developing {{c1::years}} after infection.
The oral lesion of tertiary syphilis is the {{c1::gumma}} — a destructive, {{c2::non-infectious}} granulomatous lesion that may perforate the palate.
Tertiary syphilis may involve the {{c1::heart and nervous system}} and requires medical intervention.
{{c1::Latent}} syphilis: no clinical signs or symptoms, but the person is still infected; it begins after the secondary lesions heal and can last for years.
Congenital syphilis is transmission of Treponema pallidum from an {{c1::infected mother to the fetus}}, or during birth.
{{c1::Hutchinson incisors}} are screwdriver-shaped: broad at the cervical third and narrow at the incisal edge, with a central {{c2::notch}}.
cloze.extra: Fun fact: named after Sir Jonathan Hutchinson (1828–1913), a British physician and surgeon.

cloze.text: {{c1::Mulberry molars}} have multiple enamel nodules instead of defined cusps.
Babies with congenital syphilis need immediate {{c1::penicillin}} to prevent blindness, deafness, dental abnormalities, and neurologic damage.
Hutchinson's triad: Hutchinson teeth, {{c1::interstitial keratitis}}, and {{c2::sensorineural hearing loss}}.
{{c1::Clinical}} diagnosis is based on direct visual and tactile examination of the lesion — shape, size, color, location, texture.
Fordyce granules, tori, melanin pigmentation, and lingual varicosities are usually diagnosed by {{c1::clinical}} diagnosis (just by looking).
{{c1::Radiographic}} diagnosis uses findings on dental radiographs that reveal things not seen in a visual exam.
A radiolucent area surrounding the crown of an impacted mandibular third molar suggests a {{c1::dentigerous cyst}}.
{{c1::Historical}} diagnosis is supported by the patient's medical, dental, drug, and family history.
Generalized gingival enlargement without plaque in a patient taking {{c1::phenytoin}} (an anti-seizure drug) = drug-induced gingival hyperplasia.
{{c1::Laboratory}} diagnosis involves blood or urine testing to check for systemic disease and other abnormalities.
Elevated serum {{c1::alkaline phosphatase}} may point toward {{c2::Paget's disease}}.
{{c1::Microscopic}} diagnosis examines a biopsy sample under a microscope and can be a {{c2::definitive}} diagnostic tool, especially for suspicious or precancerous lesions.

Under the microscope, invasive squamous cell carcinoma shows abnormal epithelial cells invading the {{c1::connective tissue}}, with enlarged nuclei, an increased {{c2::nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio}}, and abnormal mitotic figures.
{{c1::Surgical}} diagnosis is used when diagnosis is only possible by exploring the area surgically.
{{c1::Therapeutic}} diagnosis is made by trying a treatment and observing the response.
A {{c1::differential}} diagnosis is a list of possible conditions that could explain the findings; it helps rule out more serious issues and focuses on the most likely cause.

basic.front: Don't be confused: verruca vulgaris vs pemphigus vulgaris — what does "vulgaris" mean, and how do they differ?
basic.back: "Vulgaris" = "common" (Latin). Verruca vulgaris = common viral wart (HPV), a painless papillary growth. Pemphigus vulgaris = serious autoimmune disease with painful blisters and ulcers in the mouth and on the skin.

basic.front: A patient says her lip has been tingling since yesterday — a herpes outbreak is starting. What do you do, and why?
basic.back: Stop / reschedule the appointment. Do not treat patients with active oral herpes — even at the prodromal stage — because of viral spread through aerosols, saliva, or contact.
White, lacy, interlacing lines — the distinguishing feature of lichen planus
basic.extra: Fun fact: Louis Wickham first described these fine white lines in 1895.

basic.back: Slight lateral pressure or rubbing on normal-appearing skin or mucosa makes the outer layer shear/peel off or blister
basic.extra: Fun fact: named after Pyotr Vasilyevich Nikolsky, the Russian dermatologist who first described it.

basic.front: When should dental hygiene treatment be scheduled for a patient with cyclic neutropenia?
basic.back: During the normal neutrophil phases (not during a neutropenic episode) — plus frequent recall visits and excellent oral hygiene.
basic.extra: WakeUpMemory: like a stormy tide — you don't go surfing during a storm; wait for the calm phase.

basic.back: Teeth visible on radiographs but not erupted (seen in cleidocranial dysplasia)

typein.extra: Secondary syphilis also has widespread systemic involvement and needs penicillin.

Unilateral painful vesicles along a dermatome

mcq.question: A 19-year-old reports pain, a bad taste and difficulty opening his mouth. The tissue over his partially erupted tooth #17 is red and swollen with a little pus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcq.explanation: Pericoronitis = inflamed operculum over a partially erupted tooth, most often a mandibular third molar (#17), with pain, foul taste and trismus. Actinomycosis also follows dental procedures, but it forms firm abscesses draining through sinus tracts.

mcq.question: A complete-denture wearer complains of a burning palate. The palate under the denture is red with no white plaque. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
mcq.explanation: Erythematous candidiasis = red, burning areas with no white plaque, often under dentures — Candida isn't always white. Mucous membrane pemphigoid also causes red, painful mucosa, but it presents mainly as desquamative gingivitis, not a red denture-bearing palate.

mcq.question: A patient arrives for scaling with a cluster of painful vesicles on the lower lip that appeared this morning. What is the most appropriate action?
options: A. Proceed, but avoid the ultrasonic scaler
B. Proceed and apply topical acyclovir afterward
D. Proceed using a rubber dam
mcq.explanation: Active oral herpes (vesicle stage = most contagious) means no treatment: the virus spreads through aerosols, saliva and contact, so stop and reschedule. Avoiding the ultrasonic reduces aerosol but not spread through saliva or contact.

mcq.question: A 4-year-old has fever, sore throat and loss of appetite. Small red spots and ulcers are present only on the soft palate, tonsillar pillars and uvula; the gingiva, hands and feet are unaffected. What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcq.explanation: Herpangina (Coxsackie virus) is confined to the posterior oral cavity. Hand-foot-mouth disease is caused by the same virus but involves the tongue/buccal mucosa plus the palms and soles; primary herpes causes red, swollen gingiva.

mcq.question: Two weeks after a cold sore, a patient suddenly develops bull's-eye lesions on her hands, ulcers on the lateral tongue and crusted, bleeding lips. Which condition is most likely?
mcq.explanation: Erythema multiforme is an acute hypersensitivity reaction often triggered by herpes simplex: target skin lesions, oral ulcers and crusted bleeding lips with explosive onset. Pemphigus vulgaris is chronic, with oral blisters often appearing before skin involvement, and no target lesions.

mcq.question: Which finding best distinguishes oral lichen planus from a solitary white lesion such as leukoplakia?
options: A. It wipes off with gauze
B. Bilateral, symmetrical lacy white lines on the buccal mucosa
C. A single firm, painless ulcer
mcq.answer: B. Bilateral, symmetrical lacy white lines on the buccal mucosa
mcq.explanation: Lichen planus is bilateral and symmetrical, most often on the buccal mucosa, with white lacy Wickham's striae. A lesion that wipes off suggests candidiasis instead.

mcq.question: An older woman has peeling, inflamed gingiva and a history of eye lesions; her lesions tend to heal with scarring. Which condition is most likely?
mcq.explanation: Mucous membrane pemphigoid affects oral, ocular and genital mucosa, presents as desquamative gingivitis and heals with scarring. Pemphigus vulgaris is the more severe blistering disease with intraepithelial blisters, typically starting orally and spreading to the skin.

mcq.question: A panoramic radiograph of a 15-year-old shows many unerupted permanent and extra teeth, while few teeth are visible clinically. Which condition is most likely?
mcq.explanation: Cleidocranial dysplasia: multiple supernumerary teeth, delayed eruption and pseudoanodontia (teeth on the radiograph, not erupted). Ellis-van Creveld instead shows missing central incisors, a fused upper lip and natal teeth.

mcq.question: An HIV-positive patient has a distinct red band along the free gingival margin. Plaque is minimal and the band does not improve with improved oral hygiene. What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcq.explanation: Linear gingival erythema = red band along the gingival margin not associated with plaque (immune dysregulation). Kaposi sarcoma is a purple vascular tumor of the palate or gingiva, not a marginal band.

mcq.question: A 9-year-old has severe periodontitis with mobile permanent teeth and thick, scaly skin on the palms and soles. Which condition is most likely?
mcq.explanation: Papillon-Lefèvre = severe early periodontitis with tooth loss (often by 14) plus palmar and plantar hyperkeratosis. Cyclic neutropenia also causes rapid periodontal destruction but has no skin thickening — its ulcers come and go with neutrophil cycles.

mcq.question: Which oral lesion of syphilis is NOT infectious?
options: D. All syphilis lesions are infectious
mcq.explanation: The gumma of tertiary syphilis is destructive but non-infectious. Mucous patches (secondary) are the MOST infectious, and the chancre (primary) is highly infectious. Mnemonic C-M-G = "Cute Monkeys Giggle".

mcq.question: A patient has a white patch on the lateral border of the tongue that does not wipe off. The clinician lists leukoplakia, hairy leukoplakia, lichen planus, and candidiasis as possibilities. This list is an example of which type of diagnosis?
mcq.explanation: A differential diagnosis is the list of possible conditions that could explain the findings, used to rule out serious issues and focus on the most likely cause. Therapeutic diagnosis would be giving a treatment (e.g., nystatin) and watching the response.

mcq.question: Which lesion commonly presents with a painless, blue, dome-shaped swelling on the lower lip?
mcq.explanation: Keywords: painless, blue, dome-shaped, lower lip. A mucocele is caused by trauma to a minor salivary gland duct, leading to mucin spillage into the surrounding tissue. It presents as a soft, bluish, dome-shaped swelling, most commonly on the lower lip; it is painless and usually less than 1.5 cm.

mcq.question: Which oral lesion is most commonly associated with EBV and appears as a white, corrugated plaque on the lateral border of the tongue?
mcq.explanation: Keywords: EBV, white, corrugated plaque, lateral tongue. Hairy leukoplakia is caused by Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) and seen especially in HIV-positive or immunocompromised patients. Appears as white, corrugated (hairy) lesions on the lateral tongue that cannot be wiped off.

mcq.question: Which lesion is most likely to present as multiple small red projections on the palatal vault under a denture?
mcq.explanation: Keywords: small red projections, palatal vault, under denture. Papillary hyperplasia is caused by chronic denture wear and often Candida, especially when the denture is never removed. The palate develops many small red papillary projections, giving a cobblestone appearance.

mcq.question: Which condition presents with a strawberry-like tongue, sore throat, and fever, and may progress to scarlet fever?
mcq.explanation: Keywords: strawberry tongue, sore throat, fever, scarlet fever. Strep throat is caused by Group A Streptococcus; it presents with fever, sore throat, white tonsillar patches and in some cases strawberry tongue. Can lead to scarlet fever, a rash with sandpaper-like texture.

mcq.question: Which bone lesion shows a "sunburst" radiographic pattern and commonly presents with painful swelling in the jaws?
mcq.explanation: Keywords: sunburst, radiograph, painful swelling, jaws. Osteosarcoma is a malignant bone tumor that often affects the jaw, especially in young adults. Radiographically it may show spiculated bone radiating outwards, giving a sunburst appearance.

mcq.question: Which cyst arises from remnants of dental lamina and shows a high recurrence rate due to daughter cysts?
mcq.explanation: Keywords: dental lamina, high recurrence, daughter cysts. The odontogenic keratocyst (OKC) originates from dental lamina remnants, typically in the posterior mandible, shows a multilocular radiolucency, and has a thin, fragile lining with daughter cysts, causing high recurrence.

mcq.question: Which lesion appears radiographically as a well-defined radiolucency at the apex of a non-vital tooth and is lined by epithelium?
mcq.explanation: Keywords: radiolucency, apex, non-vital tooth, epithelial lining. The periapical cyst is the most common odontogenic cyst. Caused by pulpal necrosis activating the epithelial rests of Malassez, creating a fluid-filled, epithelium-lined cavity at the apex.

mcq.question: Which lesion is caused by chronic mechanical irritation and presents as a firm, painless, dome-shaped nodule of fibrous tissue?
mcq.explanation: Keywords: mechanical irritation, fibrous tissue, painless nodule. Irritation fibroma is a reactive lesion due to chronic trauma (e.g., cheek biting). Appears as a firm, pale pink, dome-shaped mass of dense fibrous tissue, typically on the buccal mucosa or tongue.

mcq.question: Which of the following is a benign soft tissue tumor composed of mature fat cells?
mcq.explanation: Keywords: benign tumor, fat cells. Lipoma is a benign tumor of adipose (fat) tissue, often appearing as a soft, yellowish, painless mass in the oral mucosa or submucosa.

mcq.question: Which lesion appears as a "soap-bubble" radiolucency in the posterior mandible and arises from dental lamina remnants?
mcq.explanation: Keywords: soap-bubble, posterior mandible, dental lamina. Ameloblastoma is a benign but locally aggressive odontogenic tumor that arises from dental lamina, usually in the posterior mandible, and shows a "soap-bubble" multilocular radiolucency.
